claim: The cryo-EM structure of a hamster SUR1/rat Kir6.2 channel bound to glibenclamide and ATP was determined at 3.63 Å resolution.
source: Here, we present a cryo-EM structure of a hamster SUR1/rat Kir6.2 channel bound to a high-affinity sulfonylurea drug glibenclamide and ATP at 3.63 Å resolution, which reveals unprecedented details of the ATP and glibenclamide binding sites.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the resolution and ligands present in the structure.

claim: Glibenclamide is lodged in the transmembrane bundle of the SUR1-ABC core connected to the first nucleotide binding domain near the inner leaflet of the lipid bilayer.
source: Importantly, the structure shows for the first time that glibenclamide is lodged in the transmembrane bundle of the SUR1-ABC core connected to the first nucleotide binding domain near the inner leaflet of the lipid bilayer.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the location of glibenclamide based on the structural data.

claim: Mutation of residues predicted to interact with glibenclamide led to reduced sensitivity to glibenclamide.
source: Mutation of residues predicted to interact with glibenclamide in our model led to reduced sensitivity to glibenclamide.
evidence: The abstract states that functional experiments with mutations support the structural model.

claim: KATP channels are hetero-octameric complexes composed of four Kir6 channel subunits and four sulfonylurea receptor (SUR) subunits.
source: ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channels are unique hetero-octameric complexes each composed of four inwardly rectifying Kir6 channel subunits and four sulfonylurea receptor (SUR) subunits belonging to the ATP binding cassette (ABC) transporter protein family (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999; Nichols, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In pancreatic β-cells, KATP channels formed by Kir6.2 and SUR1 are gated by intracellular ATP and ADP.
source: In pancreatic β-cells, KATP channels formed by Kir6.2 and SUR1 are gated by intracellular ATP and ADP, with ATP inhibiting channel activity while Mg2+-complexed ATP and ADP stimulating channel activity (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999; Ashcroft, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: ATP inhibits KATP channel activity.
source: In pancreatic β-cells, KATP channels formed by Kir6.2 and SUR1 are gated by intracellular ATP and ADP, with ATP inhibiting channel activity while Mg2+-complexed ATP and ADP stimulating channel activity (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999; Ashcroft, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Mg2+-complexed ATP and ADP stimulate KATP channel activity.
source: In pancreatic β-cells, KATP channels formed by Kir6.2 and SUR1 are gated by intracellular ATP and ADP, with ATP inhibiting channel activity while Mg2+-complexed ATP and ADP stimulating channel activity (Aguilar-Bryan and Bryan, 1999; Ashcroft, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: During glucose stimulation, the intracellular ATP to ADP ratio increases following glucose metabolism, which favors channel closure by ATP.
source: During glucose stimulation, the intracellular ATP to ADP ratio increases following glucose metabolism, which favors channel closure by ATP, resulting in membrane depolarization, Ca2+ influx, and exocytosis of insulin granules.
evidence: This describes the established physiological mechanism of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.

claim: KATP channel closure results in membrane depolarization, Ca2+ influx, and exocytosis of insulin granules.
source: During glucose stimulation, the intracellular ATP to ADP ratio increases following glucose metabolism, which favors channel closure by ATP, resulting in membrane depolarization, Ca2+ influx, and exocytosis of insulin granules.
evidence: This describes the established physiological mechanism of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.

claim: KATP channels control insulin secretion according to blood glucose levels.
source: In this way, KATP channels are able to control insulin secretion according to blood glucose levels.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on established physiological knowledge.

claim: Mutations that disrupt KATP channel function cause a spectrum of insulin secretion disorders.
source: Mutations that disrupt channel function are known to cause a spectrum of insulin secretion disorders (Ashcroft, 2005; Koster et al., 2005a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in KATP channels result in congenital hyperinsulinism.
source: Specifically, loss-of-function mutations result in congenital hyperinsulinism, whereas gain-of-function mutations lead to transient or permanent neonatal diabetes (Ashcroft, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Sulfonylureas were discovered in the 1940s.
source: Discovered in the 1940s, sulfonylureas have been a mainstay of type 2 diabetes therapy for more than half a century (Sola et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The authors previously determined the structure of the β-cell KATP channel complex in the presence of ATP and GBC at 5.7 Å resolution.
source: To begin to address the structural mechanisms by which ATP and sulfonylureas such as GBC inhibit KATP channels to stimulate insulin secretion, we recently carried out single particle cryo-EM and determined the structure of the β-cell KATP channel complex in the presence of ATP and GBC (Martin et al., 2017). While our initial structure at a resolution of 5.7 Å revealed the overall architecture of the channel and location of the ATP molecule, it was unable to clearly define the GBC binding site and the atomic details associated with ATP binding.
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous publication.

claim: Channels comprising rat Kir6.2 and FLAG-tagged hamster SUR1 were expressed in rat insulinoma INS-1 832/13 cells.
source: To obtain a structure of KATP channels bound to GBC and ATP, channels comprising a rat Kir6.2 and FLAG-tagged hamster SUR1 (96% and 95% sequence identity to human sequences, respectively) were expressed in rat insulinoma INS-1 832/13 cells (Hohmeier et al., 2000), affinity purified, and imaged in the presence of 1 mM ATP (no Mg2+) and 1 µM GBC, as described previously (Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Hamster SUR1 has 95% sequence identity to human SUR1.
source: To obtain a structure of KATP channels bound to GBC and ATP, channels comprising a rat Kir6.2 and FLAG-tagged hamster SUR1 (96% and 95% sequence identity to human sequences, respectively) were expressed in rat insulinoma INS-1 832/13 cells (Hohmeier et al., 2000), affinity purified, and imaged in the presence of 1 mM ATP (no Mg2+) and 1 µM GBC, as described previously (Martin et al., 2017).

claim: 3D classification in Relion yielded one four-fold symmetric class, which reached an overall resolution of 4.07 Å after refinement.
source: 3D classification in Relion yielded one four-fold symmetric class, which reached an overall resolution of 4.07 Å after refinement (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Table 1).

source: Particles from this class were further classified and refined using Frealign (Grigorieff, 2016), which yielded a map with improved resolution of 3.63 Å (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Table 1).
evidence: This describes the data processing results, with reference to figures and tables.

claim: The local resolution varied from 3.2 Å in the Kir6.2 transmembrane domain to ~5 Å in the SUR1 nucleotide binding domains.
source: The local resolution, as estimated by Bsoft, varied from 3.2 Å in the Kir6.2 transmembrane domain (TMD) to ~5 Å in the SUR1 nucleotide binding domains (NBDs) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

source: The ABC core of SUR1 displayed greater variability in resolution: the inner helices (relative to Kir6.2/TMD0) were also very well resolved (between 3.5 and 4 Å resolution) to permit nearly complete atomic model building, while the most exposed helices (TMs 9, 10, 12, and 13) showed signs of flexibility, and were only built as polyalanine chains.

claim: The NBDs of SUR1 were only refined as rigid bodies.

claim: The KATP channel is built around a tetrameric Kir6.2 core with each subunit in complex with one SUR1.
source: The KATP channel is built around a tetrameric Kir6.2 core with each subunit in complex with one SUR1 (Figure 1B–E), as observed previously (Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the overall architecture of the channel, with reference to figures and a previous publication.

claim: Each Kir6.2 has the typical Kir channel architecture of an N-terminal cytoplasmic domain, a TMD consisting of two TMs termed M1 and M2 interspersed by a pore loop and selectivity filter, and a 'tether' helix that links the TMD to the larger C-terminal cytoplasmic domain.
source: Each Kir6.2 has the typical Kir channel architecture of an N-terminal cytoplasmic domain, a TMD consisting of two TMs termed M1 and M2 interspersed by a pore loop and selectivity filter, and a 'tether' helix that links the TMD to the larger C-terminal cytoplasmic domain (CTD) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the structural features of Kir6.2, with reference to figures.

claim: Constrictions in the selectivity filter (T130), bundle crossing (F168), and the G-loop (G295, I296) indicate a closed pore.
source: In our new structure, constrictions in the selectivity filter (T130), bundle crossing (F168), and the G-loop (G295, I296) are clearly seen (Figure 2B,C) to indicate a closed pore.
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

claim: SUR1 possesses an N-terminal transmembrane domain, TMD0, in addition to an ABC core structure comprising two TMDs of 6 helices each and two cytosolic NBDs.
source: SUR1 is one of only a handful of ABC transporters which possesses an N-terminal transmembrane domain, TMD0, in addition to an ABC core structure comprising two TMDs of 6 helices each and two cytosolic NBDs (Tusnády et al., 2006; Wilkens, 2015) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This describes the structural features of SUR1, with reference to figures and citations.

claim: TMD0 is a well-resolved 5-TM bundle.
source: In the structure, TMD0 is a well-resolved 5-TM bundle (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

claim: A long intracellular loop L0 which tethers TMD0 to the ABC core is found to contain both cytosolic and amphipathic domains.
source: A long intracellular loop L0 which tethers TMD0 to the ABC core is found to contain both cytosolic and amphipathic domains (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

claim: The C-terminal 2/3 of L0 is homologous to the 'lasso motif' observed in CFTR and MRP1.
source: The C-terminal 2/3 of L0 is homologous to the 'lasso motif' observed in CFTR (Liu et al., 2017; Zhang and Chen, 2016) and MRP1 (Johnson and Chen, 2017), and indeed, the structures are very similar (Figure 2E).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures and citations.

claim: SUR1 is found in an 'inward-facing' conformation, with NBDs clearly separated and the vestibule formed by TMD1/TMD2 open towards the cytoplasm.
source: SUR1 is found in an 'inward-facing' conformation, with NBDs clearly separated and the vestibule formed by TMD1/TMD2 open towards the cytoplasm.
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The two TMD-NBDs show a ~15° rotation and ~10 Å horizontal translation relative to each other.
source: As we noted previously, the two TMD-NBDs show a ~15° rotation and ~10 Å horizontal translation relative to each other (Figure 2F) (Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to a figure and a previous publication.

claim: The lack of symmetry between the two TMD-NBDs is also seen in recently reported CFTR and MRP1 inward-facing structures.
source: This lack of symmetry is also seen in recently reported CFTR and MRP1 inward-facing structures (Johnson and Chen, 2017; Liu et al., 2017; Zhang and Chen, 2016).
evidence: This compares the current structure to other published structures.

claim: The separation between the two NBDs in the SUR1 structure is similar to that seen in MRP1 bound to its substrate leukotriene C4.
source: The separation between the two NBDs in our structure is similar to that seen in MRP1 bound to its substrate leukotriene C4 (Johnson and Chen, 2017)(see Figure 2F).
evidence: This compares the current structure to another published structure, with reference to a figure.

claim: Only NBD2 of SUR1 is capable of hydrolyzing ATP while NBD1 harbors a degenerate ATPase site.
source: Like SUR1 in which only NBD2 is capable of hydrolyzing ATP while NBD1 harbors a degenerate ATPase site, CFTR and MRP1 also have two asymmetric NBDs (Wilkens, 2015), suggesting the relative rotation and translation between the two TMD-NBD halves may be a common characteristic of ABC transporters with asymmetric NBDs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: CFTR and MRP1 also have two asymmetric NBDs.
source: Like SUR1 in which only NBD2 is capable of hydrolyzing ATP while NBD1 harbors a degenerate ATPase site, CFTR and MRP1 also have two asymmetric NBDs (Wilkens, 2015), suggesting the relative rotation and translation between the two TMD-NBD halves may be a common characteristic of ABC transporters with asymmetric NBDs.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: The relative rotation and translation between the two TMD-NBD halves may be a common characteristic of ABC transporters with asymmetric NBDs.

evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of multiple structures.

claim: Kir6.1/Kir6.2 are the only Kir channel members known to couple to an ABC transporter.
source: Among all Kir channels, Kir6.1/Kir6.2 are the only members known to couple to an ABC transporter (Hibino et al., 2010); and among all ABC transporters, SUR1/SUR2 are the only ones known to couple to an ion channel (Wilkens, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: SUR1/SUR2 are the only ABC transporters known to couple to an ion channel.
source: Among all Kir channels, Kir6.1/Kir6.2 are the only members known to couple to an ABC transporter (Hibino et al., 2010); and among all ABC transporters, SUR1/SUR2 are the only ones known to couple to an ion channel (Wilkens, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: SUR1 and Kir6.2 are co-dependent for both expression and function.
source: These proteins are also unique in that they are co-dependent for both expression and function (Inagaki et al., 1995; Zerangue et al., 1999).

source: In the structure, we find a series of hydrophobic and polar interactions mediated exclusively by TMD0 and L0 of SUR1 with Kir6.2 (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to a figure.

claim: The extracellular N-terminus of SUR1 closely contacts the turret and pore loop of Kir6.2.
source: The extracellular N-terminus of SUR1 closely contacts the turret and pore loop of Kir6.2 (Figure 3A–D), while TM1 of TMD0 and the M1 helix of Kir6.2 form a series of hydrophobic interactions running the length of the helices (Figure 3E).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

claim: TM1 of TMD0 and the M1 helix of Kir6.2 form a series of hydrophobic interactions running the length of the helices.
source: The extracellular N-terminus of SUR1 closely contacts the turret and pore loop of Kir6.2 (Figure 3A–D), while TM1 of TMD0 and the M1 helix of Kir6.2 form a series of hydrophobic interactions running the length of the helices (Figure 3E).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

claim: The intracellular loops ICL1, ICL2, and the N-terminal portion of L0 cluster around the Kir6.2 N-terminus.

evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

claim: H70 within the M1 helix of Kir6.2 forms an edge-to-face π-stacking interaction with W51 of TM1 of TMD0.
source: Among these, H70 within the M1 helix of Kir6.2 forms an edge-to-face π-stacking interaction with W51 of TM1 of TMD0 (Figure 3E), and Q57 of the Kir6.2 slide helix contacts F132 of ICL2 (Figure 3F).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

source: F132 is a well-studied permanent neonatal diabetes mutation which causes very high Po but also reduces physical interaction between TMD0 and Kir6.2 (Proks et al., 2007), supporting its role as a critical part of the interface.

source: We have previously reported the location of the ATP-binding site at the interface of the cytoplasmic N- and C-terminal domains from two adjacent subunits (Martin et al., 2017), giving four equivalent sites for the Kir6.2 tetramer.

claim: There is strong cryo-EM density for the ATP as well as surrounding residues in the current map.
source: In the current map, there is strong cryo-EM density for the ATP as well as surrounding residues (Figure 4., Figure 4—figure supplement 1), allowing for detailed analysis of the mode of ATP binding as well as the possible mechanism of inhibition.

source: The pocket itself is formed by the overlap of three distinct cytoplasmic structures: an N-terminal peptide (binding residues N48 and R50; subunit A) immediately before the Kir channel 'slide helix'; a C-terminal β-sheet (I182 and K185; subunit B) immediately following the TMD-CTD tether helix (see Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1); and a short, solvent-exposed helical segment (Y330, F333, G334; subunit B) (Figure 4C).

evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

source: Notably, sequence comparison reveals that a key difference between Kir6.2 and other Kir channels is G334, which in other Kir channels is occupied by larger amino acids.

claim: Crosslinking of Kir6.2 residue 52 and SUR1 residue 203 via a Kir6.2-Q52C and SUR1-E203C mutant pair induces spontaneous channel closure in the absence of ATP.
source: We have previously shown that engineered interactions between Kir6.2 residue 52 and SUR1 residue 203 via a Kir6.2-Q52E and SUR1-E203K ion pair increases channel sensitivity to ATP by nearly two orders of magnitude, and that crosslinking of the two residues via a Kir6.2-Q52C and SUR1-E203C mutant pair induces spontaneous channel closure in the absence of ATP (Pratt et al., 2012).

claim: Glibenclamide binds KATP channels with nM affinity.
source: GBC, also known as glyburide, is a second generation sulfonylurea that contains both a sulfonylurea moiety and a benzamido moiety, and binds KATP channels with nM affinity (Gribble and Reimann, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Early studies using chimeras of SUR1 and SUR2A suggest the involvement of TMs 14–16 in GBC binding.
source: Early studies using chimeras of SUR1 and SUR2A, which is known to have lower sensitivity to GBC than SUR1, suggest the involvement of TMs 14–16; in particular mutating S1238 in SUR1 to Y (note in some papers, this is numbered as S1237) as seen in SUR2A compromised GBC binding and inhibition (Ashfield et al., 1999; Winkler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Mutating S1238 in SUR1 to Y as seen in SUR2A compromised GBC binding and inhibition.
source: Early studies using chimeras of SUR1 and SUR2A, which is known to have lower sensitivity to GBC than SUR1, suggest the involvement of TMs 14–16; in particular mutating S1238 in SUR1 to Y (note in some papers, this is numbered as S1237) as seen in SUR2A compromised GBC binding and inhibition (Ashfield et al., 1999; Winkler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Studies using 125I-azido-GBC photolabeling implicated involvement of L0 of SUR1.
source: Subsequent studies using 125I-azido-GBC photolabeling implicated involvement of L0 of SUR1; specifically, two mutations Y230A and W232A in L0 severely compromised photolabeling of SUR1 (Vila-Carriles et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: Two mutations Y230A and W232A in L0 severely compromised photolabeling of SUR1 with 125I-azido-GBC.
source: Subsequent studies using 125I-azido-GBC photolabeling implicated involvement of L0 of SUR1; specifically, two mutations Y230A and W232A in L0 severely compromised photolabeling of SUR1 (Vila-Carriles et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: A bipartite binding pocket model was proposed in which S1238 and Y230/W232 constitute two ends of the pocket, each recognizing opposite ends of GBC.
source: These studies led to a model in which S1238 and Y230/W232 constitute two ends of a bipartite binding pocket, each recognizing opposite ends of GBC (Bryan et al., 2004; Winkler et al., 2007); however, whether one or both contribute directly to GBC binding remained unknown.
evidence: This refers to a previous model proposed in the literature.

claim: Well defined, non-protein density within the TMDs of SUR1 was found, with a size and shape which closely matches that of a GBC molecule.
source: In the current reconstruction we find well defined, non-protein density within the TMDs of SUR1, with a size and shape which closely matches that of a GBC molecule (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

claim: One end of the GBC density is in direct contact with S1238 and resembles the cyclohexyl moiety.
source: One end of the density is in direct contact with S1238 and resembles the cyclohexyl moiety long presumed to constitute the 'A' site that is abolished by the S1238Y mutation (Ashfield et al., 1999; Bryan et al., 2004).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map and relates them to previous functional data.

claim: The GBC binding pocket is contoured to precisely accommodate GBC.
source: The binding pocket is contoured to precisely accommodate GBC, and the combination of polar and hydrophobic residues help explain the sub-nM affinity of SUR1 for this sulfonylurea (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map, with reference to figures.

claim: The combination of polar and hydrophobic residues in the GBC binding pocket help explain the sub-nM affinity of SUR1 for GBC.
source: The binding pocket is contoured to precisely accommodate GBC, and the combination of polar and hydrophobic residues help explain the sub-nM affinity of SUR1 for this sulfonylurea (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

claim: R1246 and R1300 coordinate each oxygen of the sulfonyl group of GBC.
source: A primary anchor is composed of two arginine residues, R1246 and R1300, which coordinate each oxygen of the sulfonyl group.
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map.

claim: The benzene and cyclohexyl groups of GBC are stabilized by a series of hydrophobic interactions contributed by TM helices from both TMD1 (TM6, 7, 8) and TMD2 (TM16).
source: Each nitrogen of the urea moiety is coordinated by T1242 and N1245, and the adjacent benzene and cyclohexyl groups (adjacent to the sulfonyl and urea groups, respectively) are stabilized by a series of hydrophobic interactions contributed by TM helices from both TMD1 (TM6, 7, 8) and TMD2 (TM16).
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map.

source: Mutation of this residue to a tyrosine may alter interaction with GBC to compromise high affinity binding of GBC.

source: All six mutations, R306A, Y377A, N437A, T1242A, R1246A, and R1300A trafficked normally and responded as WT to metabolic inhibition (Figure 7A, B and D).

source: Strikingly, all six mutants showed significantly reduced or complete absence of inhibition at 100 nM, and five mutants (R306A, Y377, N437A, T1242, and R1246A) showed significantly reduced sensitivity compared to WT even at 1 µM GBC (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This describes functional experimental results, with reference to figures.

source: Strikingly, all six mutants showed significantly reduced or complete absence of inhibition at 100 nM, and five mutants (R306A, Y377, N437A, T1242, and R1246A) showed significantly reduced sensitivity compared to WT even at 1 µM GBC (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: This describes functional experimental results, with reference to figures.

source: Although these mutants were still sensitive to GBC inhibition, the extent of inhibition at steady-state was less compared to WT channels at 10 nM and 100 nM (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes functional experimental results, with reference to a figure.

source: Also worth noting, while inhibition of WT channels was nearly irreversible, inhibition of mutants was more reversible, consistent with the mutants having reduced affinity for GBC (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on functional experimental results.

source: Together these results provide strong functional evidence for the GBC binding pocket defined in our structure.

source: In our current structure, Y230 is too distant to interact directly with GBC.

source: However, the binding pocket is close to the L0-TMD interface, where the L0 amphipathic helix forms a series of mostly hydrophobic interactions with transmembrane helices from TMD1/2 that line the GBC binding pocket. Here, we find that Y230 stacks closely against the aliphatic portion of the R1246 side chain, which in turn coordinates an oxygen of the sulfonyl group of GBC (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).

claim: Y230 and W232 have an important but clearly indirect role in GBC binding.
source: These observations indicate an important but clearly indirect role for Y230 and W232 in GBC binding.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis.

source: The structure presented here is also in the presence of ATP and GBC and is nearly identical to the structure we published previously but with much improved resolution, allowing for accurate modelling of nearly all side-chains, many of which were absent in our previous structure (Martin et al., 2017).
evidence: This compares the current structure to the authors' previous publication.

claim: The two structures (current study and Li et al.) are very similar, both in terms of organization of the complex and conformations of Kir6.2 and SUR1 individually.
source: Overall, we find that the two structures are also very similar, both in terms of organization of the complex and conformations of Kir6.2 and SUR1 individually (Figure 8).
evidence: This compares the current structure to the structure by Li et al., with reference to a figure.

claim: Either ATP does not induce significant conformational change of the channel or GBC stabilizes the channel in a conformation that resembles an ATP-bound state.
source: Since the structure from Li et al. lacks ATP whereas our structure is bound to ATP, it suggests that either ATP does not induce significant conformational change of the channel or that GBC, which is present in both structures, stabilizes the channel in a conformation that resembles an ATP-bound state.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the two structures.

claim: GBC may stabilize the channel in a conformation that resembles an ATP-bound state, which offers a potential mechanism by which GBC inhibits channel activity.
source: The latter possibility is intriguing as it offers a potential mechanism by which GBC inhibits channel activity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Li et al. attributed GBC to unassigned density surrounding Y230 and W232.
source: In Li et al, they attributed GBC to unassigned density surrounding Y230 and W232, two residues previously proposed to be involved in sulfonylurea binding (Vila-Carriles et al., 2007).
evidence: This refers to the interpretation in the Li et al. publication.

claim: In the Li et al. structure, residues 214–222 of SUR1-L0 were not modeled.
source: However, in their structure, they did not model residues 214–222 of SUR1-L0, which happen to lie close to their 'GBC' density (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This refers to the model building in the Li et al. publication, with reference to a figure.

claim: The density attributed to GBC by Li et al. matches well to residues R216-F221 of SUR1-L0.
source: Docking our current structure into their map (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A and B, blue), we find that the density they observed matches well to those residues left out of their model, corresponding to approximately R216-F221.
evidence: This describes the authors' re-analysis of the Li et al. map, with reference to a figure.

claim: Unassigned density near the GBC binding site that corresponds to the size and shape of GBC was found in both the authors' previous 5.7 Å map and the map by Li et al.
source: Interestingly, having identified the GBC binding site using our higher resolution structure, we re-inspected our previous 5.7 Å map as well as the map by Li et al. and found unassigned density near the GBC binding site that corresponds to the size and shape of GBC in both (Figure 8—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes the authors' re-analysis of previous maps, with reference to a figure.

claim: The structure provides novel mechanistic insights of how sulfonylureas and ATP interact with the KATP channel complex to inhibit channel activity.
source: Our structure provides novel mechanistic insights of how sulfonylureas and ATP interact with the KATP channel complex to inhibit channel activity.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the significance of the work.

claim: ATP, by binding to a pocket created by the N-terminus and CTD from two adjacent Kir6.2 subunits with contributions from L0 of SUR1, acts to stabilize interactions between the Kir6.2 N-terminus and L0 to prevent movements necessary to open the channel.
source: We propose that ATP, by binding to a pocket created by the N-terminus and CTD from two adjacent Kir6.2 subunits with contributions from L0 of SUR1, acts to stabilize interactions between the Kir6.2 N-terminus and L0 to prevent movements necessary to open the channel (Figure 9A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their structural and functional data, with reference to a figure.

claim: ATP and PIP2 functionally antagonize each other through allosteric regulation.
source: Previous studies have shown that ATP and PIP2 functionally antagonize each other through allosteric regulation (Enkvetchakul et al., 2000) and that ATP can bind both closed and open channels (Enkvetchakul et al., 2001; Li et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: ATP can bind both closed and open channels.
source: Previous studies have shown that ATP and PIP2 functionally antagonize each other through allosteric regulation (Enkvetchakul et al., 2000) and that ATP can bind both closed and open channels (Enkvetchakul et al., 2001; Li et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: In the presence of MgATP/ADP, there is evidence that the NBDs of SUR1 undergo dimerization to switch the SUR1-ABC core structure from an inward-facing conformation to an outward-facing conformation to antagonize the inhibitory effect of ATP at the Kir6.2 site.
source: In the presence of MgATP/ADP, there is evidence that the NBDs of SUR1 undergo dimerization to switch the SUR1-ABC core structure from an inward-facing conformation to an outward-facing conformation to antagonize the inhibitory effect of ATP at the Kir6.2 site, and GBC binding to SUR1 stabilizes the SUR1-ABC core in an inward-facing conformation to prevent MgATP/ADP from opening the channel (Ortiz et al., 2012) (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature, with reference to a figure.

claim: GBC binding to SUR1 stabilizes the SUR1-ABC core in an inward-facing conformation to prevent MgATP/ADP from opening the channel.
source: In the presence of MgATP/ADP, there is evidence that the NBDs of SUR1 undergo dimerization to switch the SUR1-ABC core structure from an inward-facing conformation to an outward-facing conformation to antagonize the inhibitory effect of ATP at the Kir6.2 site, and GBC binding to SUR1 stabilizes the SUR1-ABC core in an inward-facing conformation to prevent MgATP/ADP from opening the channel (Ortiz et al., 2012) (Figure 9B).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature, with reference to a figure.

claim: In the absence of MgATP/ADP where the SUR1-ABC core is expected to be in an inward-facing conformation, channels are still able to open with high probability.
source: In the absence of MgATP/ADP where the SUR1-ABC core is expected to be in an inward-facing conformation, channels are still able to open with high probability (Lin et al., 2003) and GBC also causes rapid inhibition of channel activity under such a condition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting GBC can inhibit channels in a MgATP/ADP independent manner.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature and functional data, with reference to a figure.

claim: GBC causes rapid inhibition of channel activity in the absence of MgATP/ADP.
source: In the absence of MgATP/ADP where the SUR1-ABC core is expected to be in an inward-facing conformation, channels are still able to open with high probability (Lin et al., 2003) and GBC also causes rapid inhibition of channel activity under such a condition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting GBC can inhibit channels in a MgATP/ADP independent manner.
evidence: This is supported by functional data, with reference to a figure.

claim: GBC can inhibit channels in a MgATP/ADP independent manner.
source: In the absence of MgATP/ADP where the SUR1-ABC core is expected to be in an inward-facing conformation, channels are still able to open with high probability (Lin et al., 2003) and GBC also causes rapid inhibition of channel activity under such a condition (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), suggesting GBC can inhibit channels in a MgATP/ADP independent manner.
evidence: This is an inference based on functional data.

claim: GBC may inhibit channel activity in the absence of MgATP/ADP by modulating interactions between the distal N-terminus of Kir6.2 and SUR1.
source: While the mechanism by which GBC inhibits channel activity in the absence of MgATP/ADP is not clear, we hypothesize that it may involve modulating interactions between the distal N-terminus of Kir6.2 and SUR1.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The distal N-terminal 30 amino acids of Kir6.2 have been shown to be important for the binding or effect of GBC.
source: The distal N-terminal 30 amino acids of Kir6.2 have been shown to be important for the binding or effect of GBC in a number of studies (Devaraneni et al., 2015; Koster et al., 1999; Kühner et al., 2012; Reimann et al., 1999; Vila-Carriles et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: The distal N-terminus of Kir6.2 is involved in regulating channel open probability by interacting with L0 of SUR1.
source: Moreover, it is known to be involved in regulating channel open probability by interacting with L0 of SUR1 (Babenko et al., 1999; Shyng et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: There is a lack of strong density N-terminal to position 32 of Kir6.2 in the map, suggesting this region is flexible.
source: In our map, there is a lack of strong density N-terminal to position 32 of Kir6.2, suggesting this region is flexible.
evidence: This describes structural features observed in the cryo-EM map and infers flexibility.

claim: GBC increased crosslinking of Kir6.2 to SUR1 when Azido-p-phenylalanine was placed at the distal N-terminus of Kir6.2 (amino acid position 12 or 18).
source: However, it is worth noting that our previous study using engineered unnatural amino acid Azido-p-phenylalanine placed at the distal N-terminus of Kir6.2 (amino acid position 12 or 18) has demonstrated that GBC increased crosslinking of Kir6.2 to SUR1 (Devaraneni et al., 2015).
evidence: This refers to the authors' previous publication.

claim: GBC binding to the TMD bundle next to the L0 amphipathic helix of SUR1 stabilizes the interactions between the N-terminus of Kir6.2 and SUR1 to prevent the movement of Kir6.2 N-terminus that is needed to open the gate.
source: Thus, we hypothesize that GBC binding to the TMD bundle next to the L0 amphipathic helix of SUR1 stabilizes the interactions between the N-terminus of Kir6.2 and SUR1 to prevent the movement of Kir6.2 N-terminus that is needed to open the gate (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their structural and functional data, with reference to a figure.

claim: Channels exposed to saturating concentrations of GBC can be further inhibited by addition of ATP.
source: Although GBC is a potent inhibitor of KATP channels, it does not completely eliminate channel activity, unlike ATP. Channels exposed to saturating concentrations of GBC can be further inhibited by addition of ATP (see Figure 7—figure supplement 1A; Figure 8B).
